assessment.1. Complaint structure: direct interfere: This case concerns a direct State interference with the applicant’s freedom of expression, not a positive-obligation issue. Although the domestic authorities framed the matter as terrorism-related criminal proceedings, the practical basis of the measures included the applicant’s speeches, conference participation, interviews, press statements and participation in demonstrations in her capacity as a prominent opposition politician and DTK co-chair (see paragraphs 13, 15, 18, 28-30, 54). Her arrest, pre-trial detention, prosecution and eventual conviction were all capable of seriously chilling her future expression and that of other political actors (see paragraphs 23, 32-45, 47). Pre-trial detention based on expressive activities is itself an interference requiring very careful scrutiny (see no. 23199/17).

assessment.2. Nature of the speech and margin of ap: The impugned expression lay at the core of Article 10 protection. The applicant was a well-known political figure, former member of parliament and deputy chair of the HDP, speaking on the Kurdish issue, democratic autonomy, protest methods and the resolution process in Türkiye (see paragraphs 6-8, 28). These are matters of the highest public interest, so the State’s margin of appreciation was narrow. Strasbourg case-law gives especially strong protection to opposition politicians and to debate on sensitive political questions, including Kurdish-related issues, unless the speech can reasonably be read as inciting violence, armed resistance or hatred (see nos. 31451/03, 67360/11). Here, the summaries show that the applicant advocated a political-administrative model, said civil disobedience could be a democratic means, and argued that the PKK and Abdullah Öcalan should be included in a resolution process (see paragraph 28). On their face, those statements are political opinions, not calls to violence.

assessment.3. Lawfulness and legitimate aim: There was a formal legal basis in domestic law, namely Article 314 of the Criminal Code and the detention provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraphs 16, 19, 23, 50, 61). The measures also pursued aims that can fall within Article 10 § 2, especially national security and prevention of disorder or crime, given the authorities’ reliance on alleged PKK/KCK links (see paragraphs 17-19, 50-52). That said, the application of those provisions raises foreseeability concerns because neither the prosecutor’s questioning nor the indictment clearly identified which precise statements were said to be criminal; the file expressly notes that no specific statements were identified during questioning, and the indictment reproduced numerous speeches without specifying which passages constituted an offence (see paragraphs 15 and 28). Still, even assuming the interference was prescribed by law and pursued legitimate aims, the decisive issue is necessity and proportionality.

assessment.4. Necessity: lack of relevant and suffi: The domestic authorities did not provide relevant and sufficient reasons showing a pressing social need to penalise the applicant’s expression. First, the detention order and indictment relied heavily on her institutional role in the DTK and broadly assumed that the DTK was part of the PKK/KCK structure, instead of demonstrating how her own words or conduct promoted terrorist violence (see paragraphs 17-18, 23-25, 27-30). The magistrate even treated her description of the DTK as a civil platform as an implicit admission of guilt, which is not a Convention-compliant assessment of political speech (see paragraph 24). Second, the authorities grouped together lawful political activity with incriminating allegations: attendance at public meetings, a conference in the Swiss Parliament, interviews on a television channel, peaceful demonstrations and press statements were all presented as evidence of terrorism without any concrete analysis of content, context, audience or risk (see paragraphs 18, 21, 28-30). Third, the national courts never identified any statement by the applicant that incited violence or hatred, praised armed attacks, or could realistically trigger public disorder. This omission is decisive in anti-terror cases concerning political speech (see nos. 31451/03, 67360/11).

assessment.5. Failure of Convention-compliant balan: The domestic courts and the Constitutional Court failed to conduct the balancing exercise required by Article 10. Their reasoning rested mainly on the seriousness of the charge, the catalogue-offence nature of the offence, and abstract references to evidence, absconding risk and tampering risk (see paragraphs 25, 32-43, 50-55). They did not engage with the essential Article 10 questions: whether the statements contributed to a debate of public interest, whether they were factual assertions or value judgments, whether they had a sufficient factual basis, whether they endorsed violence, and whether less restrictive measures could protect the legitimate aims pursued. The Constitutional Court merely referred back to the detention reasoning and dismissed the Article 10 complaint as manifestly ill-founded (see paragraphs 54-55). Such formulaic reasoning falls short of the strict scrutiny required where criminal-law measures affect political expression (see no. 23199/17).

assessment.6. Proportionality and chilling effect: The severity of the measures was manifestly disproportionate. The applicant was arrested, kept in lengthy pre-trial detention, then sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment for membership of an armed organisation (see paragraphs 11, 23, 32-45, 47). Even though the trial court ultimately found no evidence that she had distributed roles, exercised authority, planned activities or controlled the organisation, it still convicted her of membership (see paragraph 44). This weakens the State’s justification for having treated her public speech and political activities as criminal from the outset. Long detention and a heavy prison sentence imposed in response to political expression have an obvious chilling effect not only on the applicant but on democratic debate generally, especially for opposition voices on contentious public issues (see nos. 16483/12, 23199/17). In the absence of demonstrated incitement to violence, such severe sanctions cannot be regarded as necessary in a democratic society.

assessment.7. Overall conclusion: The interference targeted core political expression on matters of public interest. Even if it had a basis in law and pursued legitimate aims, the authorities did not show that the applicant’s speeches, interviews and peaceful political activities amounted to incitement to violence or otherwise justified criminal repression. The domestic courts failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons and imposed exceptionally severe measures with a strong chilling effect. An Article 10 violation is therefore likely.
